nameStory: The 'fly' in fly-honeysuckle doesn't refer to buzzing insects, but rather to the way this shrub's small berries seem to 'fly' away quickly—they're gobbled up so fast by hungry birds like robins and cardinals! The 'American' part distinguishes our native species from the many non-native honeysuckles that have invaded New England forests.
description: American fly-honeysuckle is a native shrub that grows 3-6 feet tall in New England's woodlands. Unlike the aggressive invasive honeysuckles you might know, this well-behaved native has a graceful, open branching pattern and stays put where you plant it. It produces small, paired yellowish flowers in late spring, followed by bright red berries that birds absolutely love.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves grow in opposite pairs along the stems, feeling smooth to the touch with a slightly fuzzy texture on the underside. They're about 2-4 inches long with a pointed tip and smooth edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, tubular yellowish-white flowers appear in pairs from the leaf joints, looking like tiny trumpets about half an inch long. They have a sweet, delicate fragrance that's much subtler than invasive honeysuckles.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red berries appear in pairs joined at their bases, creating a distinctive 'twin berry' look that's unique among New England honeysuckles. The berries are about 1/4 inch across and taste mildly sweet.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms an open, airy shrub with ascending branches that don't create dense thickets like invasive honeysuckles. The overall shape is graceful and upright rather than sprawling.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and reddish-brown, while older stems develop light brown, fibrous bark with shallow furrows. The bark doesn't peel or flake off in strips.

habitat: Look for American fly-honeysuckle in the understory of mixed hardwood forests, especially on slopes and well-drained woodland areas. It thrives in the dappled shade beneath maples, oaks, and birches, occasionally venturing into moister spots near streams or even coniferous swamps.

seasonality.spring: Small paired flowers bloom from late April through May, filling the air with a subtle sweet fragrance. New leaves emerge bright green and soft to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Bright red twin berries ripen in early June and are quickly eaten by birds through July. The green foliage provides a nice backdrop in the forest understory.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to yellowish-green before dropping, and the shrub's open branching structure becomes more visible as surrounding plants go dormant.
seasonality.winter: The graceful branch pattern is visible, with light brown furrowed bark and small buds that help distinguish it from other woody plants.

funFact: This native honeysuckle is so rare in some states that it's listed as endangered in Maryland and New Jersey—making it more precious than many tropical orchids in those areas!
confusionNotes: The key difference from invasive honeysuckles is the paired berries that are joined at their base—invasives have separate berries. Also, native fly-honeysuckle forms open, well-behaved clumps while invasives create dense, choking thickets. Memory trick: 'Native twins stick together' (the paired berries), while 'invasive singles spread out' (separate berries and aggressive growth).
contextualKnowledge: Many people assume all honeysuckles are invasive weeds, but American fly-honeysuckle is actually a valuable native plant that's been declining due to habitat loss and competition from its invasive cousins. Supporting this native species helps restore the natural balance that our local birds and wildlife depend on.
compareHints: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit. While invasive honeysuckles often have white or pink flowers and form dense stands, our native species has yellowish flowers and grows as scattered individuals in the forest understory.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
